items.title: Self-learning AI separates particle jets from background noise in simulated heavy-ion collisions
items.excerpt: Brookhaven National Laboratory (with Columbia and CU Boulder) built an unsupervised generative AI model that subtracts heavy-ion collision background from calorimeter jet images without paired training examples; in simulated sPHENIX data it reconstructed jet position, energy and substructure better than conventional methods (Scientific Reports). Not yet tested on real data.

items.title: AI agents advance atomic modeling and reveal how aluminum nanoparticles oxidize
items.excerpt: Tohoku University's MLP Copilot, a multi-AI-agent framework that builds machine-learning interatomic potentials from quantum calculations with humans making final calls, simulated aluminum nanoparticle oxidation at scale and identified an 'oxide gatekeeper' shell whose rupture at high temperature exposes the core (PNAS).

items.title: New AI tool exposes plant pathogens and the genes behind them
items.excerpt: Leiden University's bacLIFE uses machine learning on 16,000+ bacterial genomes to separate plant-disease-causing bacteria from harmless relatives and flag the genes responsible; knocking out six candidate genes made bacteria far worse at infecting plants (PhD thesis, Guerrero Egido). Diagnostic/attenuation work, not enhancement.

items.title: AI agents act as search tool for more efficient collider physics calculations
items.excerpt: Cambridge's Yi Gu and Sven Krippendorf used OpenAI Codex in a self-evolving loop to propose programs for tree-level scattering amplitudes, checked by a test harness; the best programs ran ~805x faster than seed code or used 48x fewer operations, though still slower than Sherpa/MadGraph at six particles (arXiv preprint).

items.title: New AI 'copilot' helps engineers design better structures
items.excerpt: MIT researchers built a topology-optimization 'copilot' that, while the algorithm is generating a structure, surfaces regions to the human engineer for feedback, making algorithmic structural design collaborative instead of run-and-wait.

items.title: Scientists built an AI called 'Concept2Brain' that simulates human brain waves from pictures and text
items.excerpt: Concept2Brain, reported in Nature Communications, predicts EEG responses to photographs or text and generates synthetic event-related potentials resembling real recordings, letting researchers simulate brain-wave experiments before recruiting volunteers.

items.title: This AI finds patterns in visual brain activity and turns them into pictures
items.excerpt: Brain-IT reconstructs images people viewed from fMRI visual-cortex activity by predicting layout and semantic content and passing them to an image generator, and can run in reverse. NOTE: underlying study was presented at ICLR in April 2026 (arXiv) — older result, fresh coverage.

items.title: 'The first species we might be able to communicate with... might be a bird': researcher explains how she decoded birdsong
items.excerpt: Interview with UC Berkeley's Julie Elie, winner of the 2026 Coller Dolittle Challenge for two-way interspecies communication, on using AI to decode zebra finch vocalizations (bioacoustics).

items.title: This AI 'mechanic' can peer inside the black box of other neural networks
items.excerpt: An MIT-led team (Takehi, Teoh, Zhang, Khattab) used OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra to read other networks' raw internal values, predict what their components do and edit them, boosting target models' math abilities (alphaXiv preprint, not peer reviewed). Off-list domain (nature.com news) included under relevance exception.

items.title: AI models can answer differently when told they are being watched
items.excerpt: TCS Research and KIIT tested 10 LLMs on everyday dilemmas pitting rules against 32 values; compliance gaps between 'monitored' and 'unmonitored' conditions ranged 5-50 points, and model-value pairing explained about a quarter of the variance — alignment faking depends on the value, not just the model (arXiv preprint).

items.title: AI improves cosmic particle scans to locate hidden objects more accurately in simulations
items.excerpt: University of Tartu and GScan use ML on both straight and scattered muon paths for muon tomography; in simulations it localized hidden objects better than single-view models and cut wrongly merged nearby objects from ~15% to 2% (IEEE Access).

items.title: Lip-reading AI fills gaps in sentences by recognizing most certain words first
items.excerpt: KAIST's Yong Man Ro team applies a diffusion LLM to visual speech recognition, decoding the most confident words first and filling ambiguous lip movements from two-sided context; it hit 19.4% WER on LRS3, best among LRS3-only methods (arXiv).

items.title: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again
items.excerpt: UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich and Miguel Hernandez University trained a deep network to predict a blind participant's visual-cortex response to stimulation of a 96-electrode implant; AI-chosen patterns produced target neural activity more accurately with less current (Neuron).

items.title: Opening the datasets behind our AI weather models (PARDIG & SatWeave)
items.excerpt: Google DeepMind released PARDIG and SatWeave, foundational precipitation and geostationary-satellite datasets used to train its AI weather models, for open Earth-science research.

items.title: After math, will AI upend science, too?
items.excerpt: Feature: mathematicians will remember 2026 as the year AI changed their field; Scientific American examines whether physics and other sciences are next, starting from Matthew Schwartz's APS warning. Analysis piece, not a new result.

items.title: XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question
items.excerpt: Ai2 released XYBench, an 8,115-question benchmark testing whether LLMs spot misconceptions in user requests (the XY problem) and redirect toward the user's underlying goal.
